```{r setup, include=FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(echo = TRUE)
```
This tutorial explores the use of NEON breeding landbird data for occupancy modeling. The focus is on preparing observational bird data, constructing detection histories, and fitting single- and multi-season occupancy models. Although birds are used here as the example, the same workflow can be applied to other organismal <a href="https://www.neonscience.org/data-collection/observational-sampling" target="_blank">NEON observational sampling datasets</a> that provide species-level detections. If you are interested in linking occupancy results with environmental predictors, the methods demonstrated here can also be extended to incorporate covariates from NEON data products that describe habitat structure or climate, such as those derived from <a href="https://www.neonscience.org/data-collection/automated-instruments" target="_blank">NEON's Automated Instrument Systems</a>.
<div id="ds-objectives" markdown="1">

## Learning Objectives 
After completing this tutorial you will be able to: 

* Understand the basics of occupancy modeling.
* Prepare NEON breeding landbird data for occupancy analysis and build detection histories.
* Fit occupancy models in R and interpret occupancy and detection estimates.
* Incorporate site-level and survey-level covariates to evaluate factors influencing detection and occupancy.

## Things You’ll Need To Complete This Tutorial

### R Programming Language
You will need a current version of R to complete this tutorial. We also recommend 
the RStudio IDE to work with R. 

</div>

## Introduction to NEON Bird Observations
NEON’s breeding landbird point count dataset provides taxonomic identifications, distances, and detection information for all birds observed during standardized six-minute surveys. The protocol focuses on diurnal, terrestrial breeding landbirds, a group chosen because they respond strongly to changes in climate, habitat, and land use, and because they interact with other NEON-monitored organisms.

Field crews survey spatially distributed locations during the breeding season, recording every bird seen or heard. These repeated surveys across years and sites produce rich detection–nondetection data suited for occupancy modeling and for exploring how bird communities vary across environmental gradients.

NEON’s terrestrial field **sites** are designated as *large* or *small*, which determines the sampling design. Large sites are surveyed once per year and contain 5–10 **plots** containing Bird Grids, each made up of a 3×3 array of nine **points** spaced 250 m apart (see Figure). Field crews visit every point in a grid and conduct a 6-minute **point-count survey**. Smaller sites, which cannot accommodate full grids, are surveyed twice per year and contain 2–25 point-count locations that are randomly distributed across the site and spaced at least 250 m apart.

<div id="ds-dataTip" markdown="1">
<i class="fa fa-star"></i> **Data Tip:** NEON’s bird data follow a hierarchical structure: DomainID → SiteID → PlotID → PointID. Large sites use points labeled 1–9, while small sites use point label 21 for all locations.
For example: (Large Site) D07 → GRSM → GRSM_002 → 5 | (Small Site) D20 → PUUM → PUUM_001 → 21.
</div> 

<figure>
	<a href="https://raw.githubusercontent.com/anushkakg/Bird-Occupancy-Modeling/refs/heads/main/images/birdGrid.jpg">
	<img src="https://raw.githubusercontent.com/anushkakg/Bird-Occupancy-Modeling/refs/heads/main/images/birdGrid.jpg" alt="Design of the bird point count grid, consisting of 9 points separated by a minimum of 250 m."></a>
	<figcaption> Design of a bird grid, consisting of 9 points separated by a minimum of 250 m. Source: National Ecological Observatory Network, CC-BY (NEON)  
	</figcaption>
</figure>


More details on NEON’s bird monitoring program are available on the <a href="https://www.neonscience.org/data-collection/birds" target="_blank">NEON bird resource page</a>. Protocols referenced in the data can be found in the <a href="https://data.neonscience.org/documents" target="_blank">Document Library</a>.

Because NEON surveys are standardized in duration, timing, and protocol, differences in detection among surveys can be reasonably attributed to biological and environmental variation rather than inconsistent sampling effort. This makes the dataset especially well suited for modeling detection probability explicitly.

## Introduction to Occupancy Modeling
When searching for a species, there are technically three possible outcomes:

1. The species is present and you detect it,
2. the species is present and you do not detect it, or
3. the species is absent and therefore not detected.

Traditional presence–absence data cannot distinguish missed detections from true absences, which introduces uncertainty. Occupancy modeling addresses this challenge by explicitly modeling two linked processes: the true **occupancy** of the species and the **probability** of detecting the species given that it is present.
A key assumption of occupancy modeling is closure during the sampling period: the true occupancy state of a site does not change between repeated surveys used to estimate detection probability. In practice, this means we assume no colonization or local extinction occurs within a season (single-season models), or within each primary period (multi-season models).

This framework estimates two key parameters:

* the probability that a site is occupied by a species (ψ)
* the probability of detecting the species during a survey, given that it is present (p). 

To tease apart ψ and p, the model requires repeated surveys of the same site within a period when occupancy of a species is assumed not to change. NEON’s observational sampling design is ideal for this approach, because surveys include repeated, standardized visits to locations across years. 

## Setup R Environment

We'll need several R packages in this tutorial. Install the packages, if not already installed, and load the libraries for each. 

```{r install, eval=FALSE}

# run once to get the package, and re-run if you need to get updates
install.packages("neonUtilities") # work with NEON data
install.packages('RPresence',repo='https://www.mbr-pwrc.usgs.gov/mbrCRAN') # library for doing occupancy modelling
install.packages("dplyr") # data manipulation
install.packages("tidyr") # data reshaping and tidying
install.packages("stringr") # string handling and text processing
install.packages("ggplot2") # visualization and plotting

```

### Occupancy Modeling
NEON’s terrestrial field **sites** are designated as *large* or *small*, which determines the sampling design. Large sites are surveyed once per year and contain 5–10 **plots** containing Bird Grids, each made up of a 3×3 array of nine **points** spaced 250 m apart (see Figure). Field crews visit every point in a grid and conduct a 6-minute **point-count survey**. Smaller sites, which cannot accommodate full grids, are surveyed twice per year and contain 2–25 point-count locations that are randomly distributed across the site and spaced at least 250 m apart.

<div id="ds-dataTip" markdown="1">
<i class="fa fa-star"></i> **Data Tip:** NEON’s bird data follow a hierarchical structure: DomainID → SiteID → PlotID → PointID. Large sites use points labeled 1–9, while small sites use point label 21 for all locations.
For example: (Large Site) D07 → GRSM → GRSM_002 → 5 | (Small Site) D20 → PUUM → PUUM_001 → 21.
</div> 

A problem when studying wildlife populations is that it is impossible for wildlife species to be detected 100% of the time they are present. Therefore presence/absence data is inevitably distorted by detectability and a documented absence could mean:
1. The species is present, and we did not detect it
2. The species is not present, and we did not detect it

Occupancy models can solve this by estimating detectability of a species using data from repeated observations at each site. 


### Setup

#### Importing libraries

```{r, message=FALSE}
library(neonUtilities) #package for downloading NEON data 
library(RPresence) # library for doing occupancy modelling
library(dplyr)
library(tidyr)
library(stringr)
library(ggplot2) # library for visualization
```

#### Importing NEON Data
The method common sampling method is point counts, which involves an observer standing at a point for a predetermined amount of time, typically during the peak of singing activity, and recording all of the individuals seen or heard. 

Most NEON sites have 5-10 Bird Grids and sampling occurs once or twice per breeding season at each point at a site, depending on the size of the site. Large sites are sampled one per season, while small sites (ones that cannot accommodate the minimum of five 9-point grids) are sampled twice. We will separate large and small sites to account for this. 
```{r}
large_sites <- c(
  "BARR", "BART", "BONA", "CLBJ", "CPER", "DEJU", "DSNY", "GRSM",
  "GUAN", "HARV", "HEAL", "JERC", "JORN", "KONZ", "MLBS", "MOAB",
  "NIWO", "OAES", "ONAQ", "ORNL", "OSBS", "RMNP", "SJER", "SRER",
  "STEI", "TALL", "TEAK", "UKFS", "UNDE", "WOOD", "WREF", "YELL"
)
small_sites <- c(
  "DELA", "LENO", "TOOL", "SOAP", "STER", "PUUM", "KONA",
  "SERC", "DCFS", "NOGP", "LAJA", "BLAN", "SCBI", "ABBY", "TREE"
)
sites <- c(large_sites, small_sites)

if (!dir.exists("data")) {
  dir.create("data")
}

if (!dir.exists("outputs")) {
  dir.create("outputs")
}

if (file.exists("data/bird_counts.RData")) {
  load("data/bird_counts.RData")
} else {
  
  
  ###todo: add NEON token
  bird.counts <- loadByProduct(dpID="DP1.10003.001",
                               site=sites,
                               startdate="2018-01",
                               enddate="2023-12",
                               check.size = F)
  
  save(bird.counts, file = "data/bird_counts.RData")
}
```

#### Data Preparation
Occupancy modeling requires detection–nondetection data organized as repeated surveys at fixed locations. Raw NEON bird data are stored in a long format with one row per observation, so our primary task is to (1) uniquely identify surveys, (2) ensure surveys are comparable across space and time, and (3) reshape the data into detection histories suitable for modeling.

1. Create unique surveyID - we have to create a unique key first consisting of the site, plot, point, year and bout)

NEON’s breeding landbird point count dataset contains two data packages that are important to us: 
* brd_countdata: Point Count Data containing the actual observations (e.g., number of birds, species, distance from observer)
* brd_perpoint: Per point metadata about the survey location and conditions

```{r}
brd_countdata_clean <- bird.counts$brd_countdata %>%
  mutate(year = str_extract(eventID, "\\d{4}"))%>%
  mutate(pointSurveyID = paste(plotID, "point", pointID, year, "bout", boutNumber, sep = "_")) %>%
  mutate(locationID = paste(plotID, "point", pointID, sep = "_")) %>%
  mutate(timeID = paste(year, "bout", boutNumber, sep = "_"))

brd_perpoint_clean <- bird.counts$brd_perpoint %>%
  mutate(year = str_extract(eventID, "\\d{4}"))%>%
  mutate(pointSurveyID = paste(plotID, "point", pointID, year, "bout", boutNumber, sep = "_")) %>%
  mutate(locationID = paste(plotID, "point", pointID, sep = "_")) %>%
  mutate(timeID = paste(year, "bout", boutNumber, sep = "_"))
```

For large sites, a complete plot survey must include all nine point-count locations. Missing one or more points indicates that the survey was not completed as designed, which could bias detection probabilities. Rather than attempting to partially correct these surveys, we remove them entirely to preserve consistency.

```{r eval=FALSE, include=FALSE}
bad_pointSurveyID <- brd_perpoint_clean %>%
  filter(pointID != "21") %>%
  group_by(plotID, year, boutNumber) %>%
  filter(n_distinct(pointID) != 9) %>%
  arrange(plotID, year, boutNumber, pointID) %>%
  pull(pointSurveyID)

bad_pointSurveyID

brd_perpoint_clean <- brd_perpoint_clean %>%
  filter(!pointSurveyID %in% bad_pointSurveyID)

brd_countdata_clean <- brd_countdata_clean %>%
  filter(!pointSurveyID %in% bad_pointSurveyID)

```

2. Filter out surveys where they could not complete sampling.

```{r}
brd_perpoint_clean <- brd_perpoint_clean %>%
  filter(samplingImpractical == "OK")
```

3. Since we're only interested in species level data, we need to remove records that are not recorded to the species level or had no records for that pointSurvey minute (taxonRank will be NA)

```{r}
brd_countdata_clean <- brd_countdata_clean %>%
  filter(taxonRank == "species")
```

Sometimes there are duplicate pointSurveyIDs and there shouldn't be - this is likely due to errors in data input, so we will remove those as well. 

```{r}
duplicate_pointSurveyID <- brd_perpoint_clean %>%
  count(pointSurveyID) %>%
  filter(n > 1) %>%
  pull(pointSurveyID)

duplicate_pointSurveyID

#remove both of the duplicate surveys from each table
brd_perpoint_clean <- brd_perpoint_clean %>%
  filter(!pointSurveyID %in% duplicate_pointSurveyID)

brd_countdata_clean <- brd_countdata_clean %>%
  filter(!pointSurveyID %in% duplicate_pointSurveyID)
```

Now we will join the the point count data and the per point metadata so we have one table with all the information we need. At this stage, each row represents a species observation during a specific point-count survey, with associated environmental and survey metadata. 

```{r}
brd_joineddata_clean <- inner_join(
  brd_countdata_clean,
  brd_perpoint_clean,
  by = "pointSurveyID",
  suffix = c(".count", ".perpoint")
)

#Remove duplicate columns between tables
brd_joineddata_clean <- brd_joineddata_clean %>%
  select(-matches("\\.perpoint$"))
names(brd_joineddata_clean) <- gsub("\\.count$", "", names(brd_joineddata_clean))
```

## Descriptive Analyses

Now that our data are cleaned and standardized, we can start doing some basic analyses. 
Occupancy models can be classified into single-season or multi-season analysis. 

### Single-season Occupancy Model
We begin with a single-season occupancy model, which assumes that occupancy does not change within the sampling window. This approach is appropriate when repeated surveys occur within a relatively short time frame, such as a single breeding season. 

#### Single Species

Single species occupancy modeling monitors a target species at N sites, where the target is present at some of them. We use Melanerpes carolinus (Red-bellied Woodpecker) as an example because it is widespread, frequently detected, and occurs across many NEON sites. These characteristics make it well suited for demonstrating occupancy modeling without complications arising from sparse detections.

##### Data Munging

##### Occupancy Table
For occupancy modeling, we are we are interested in two things. 
1. Is the target present at a site? 
2. For targets that are present, is the target detected by an observer? 
The data we have pertaines to the latter, the detection of a target species across surveys. Here, we will formulate our data into a table representing the encounter history of a species where 1 represents the detection of the target. Under the assumption that occupancy patterns are fixed between the surveys, we can use this history to understand the presence or absence of the target. 

First, we will construct an occupancy table where rows represent distinct survey sites and columns represent repeated visits. In occupancy modeling, we do not model counts directly. Instead, we model whether a species was detected (1) or not detected (0) during each survey. Multiple detections within a survey are collapsed into a single detection event.

```{r}
# Filter table by species
bird_species <- "Melanerpes carolinus"
brd_joineddata_model1 <- brd_joineddata_clean %>%
  filter(siteID %in% sites) %>%
  filter(scientificName == bird_species)

# Get all valid surveys years across sites (so we can fill in NAs)
valid_site_years <- brd_perpoint_clean %>%
  distinct(siteID, year)

# Get detections — only species *actually observed at a site* (so we can fill in 0s)
detections <- brd_joineddata_model1 %>%
  group_by(siteID, year) %>%
  summarize(present = 1, .groups = "drop")

# Join and fill
site_by_year <- valid_site_years %>%
  left_join(detections, by = c("siteID", "year")) %>%
  mutate(present = replace_na(present, 0)) %>%
  pivot_wider(
    names_from = year,
    values_from = present
  )

head(site_by_year, n=10)
```

#### Create the Pao presence-absence object (Pao)
Using our detection history, we can create an R object of class “pao” (presence-absence object), which is the basic input for analysis in RPresence. The createPao() function converts the detection history matrix into a format recognized by RPresence. Each row corresponds to a site, and each column corresponds to a repeated survey. Missing values (NA) indicate that a site was not surveyed during a given year, while zeros indicate non-detections during completed surveys. For more information, consult the function's help page.

```{r}
birds_pao_model1 <- createPao(
  data = site_by_year[, c("2018", "2019", "2020", "2021", "2022", "2023")],
  unitnames = site_by_year$siteID,
  title = "Red-bellied Woodpecker"
)
```

#### Run the actual model
Using our “pao” object, we can now run the single season occupancy analysis using the RPresence function occMod(). 
The arguments to the occMod() function are: 
- model: a list of formula for each parameter, where p = detection probability and psi = occupancy
- data: pao data object
- type: a string indicating the type of occupancy model to fit

We need a formula for psi and for p. Because we do not have an independent variable and the detection probability is assumed constant across surveys, we will use psi ~ 1 and p ~ 1. 

We are conducting a single season analysis, so we will use "so," short for “static occupancy”
for the "type" argument. The alternative would be "dynamic occupancy" or multi-season. In this initial model, we assume both occupancy (ψ) and detection probability (p) are constant across all sites and surveys. While this is biologically simplistic, it provides a baseline model against which more complex models can be compared.

```{r}
birds_occupancy_model1 <- occMod(
  data = birds_pao_model1,           
  model = list(
    psi ~ 1,  
    p ~ 1),
  type = 'so'
  )

summary(birds_occupancy_model1)
```
The output shows us the AIC and the -2 log-likelihood value. The AIC (Akaike Information Criterion) measures the likelihood of each model to have generated the observed data, with a lower value being preferable. 

It also shows -2*log-likelihood, which measured the goodness of fit and is used to calculate the AIC. 

#### Model Results

Examining our results further, we see that Melanerpes carolinus has an occupancy probability (psi) of 45% (i.e., if you go to any of these sites, there is a 45% chance of this bird occupying the site) and a detection probability (p) of 91% (i.e., if you visit a site and the bird occupies it, there is a 91% chance you will detect it)

```{r}
ests <- as.data.frame(print_one_site_estimates(mod = birds_occupancy_model1))

ests <- ests[1:2,] %>% 
  mutate(parm = c("psi", "p")) %>% 
  select(parm, est, se, lower, upper) %>% 
  rename(., 
    c(
      Parameter = parm,
      Estimate = est,
      SE = se,
      L95 = lower,
      U95 = upper
    )
  ) %>% 
  `rownames<-`(seq_len(nrow(ests[1:2,])))

ests
```

```{r}
ggplot(ests, aes(x = Parameter, y = Estimate)) +
  labs(x = "Parameter", y = "Estimate") +
  geom_bar(stat = 'identity') +
  geom_errorbar(aes(ymin = L95, ymax = U95), width = 0.2) +
  theme_bw()
```

### Across all Species

#### Create a function
Now that we have demonstrated a simple occupancy model, we can write a function that applies to all species in our data. Extending this analysis across all species allows us to compare occupancy and detection patterns community-wide.

```{r, message=FALSE}
run_occ_for_species_list <- function(species_df, brd_joineddata_clean, brd_perpoint_clean, sites, years = c("2018", "2019", "2020", "2021", "2022", "2023")) {
  
  results <- list()
  detection_histories <- list()
  
  for (i in seq_len(nrow(species_df))) {
    
    sci_name <- species_df$scientificName[i]
    common_name <- species_df$vernacularName[i]
    
    # Filter detection data to this species and the sites
    brd_species <- brd_joineddata_clean %>%
      filter(siteID %in% sites, scientificName == sci_name)
    
    # Get valid surveys (site-year combos with effort)
    valid_site_years <- brd_perpoint_clean %>%
      filter(siteID %in% sites) %>%
      distinct(siteID, year)
    
    # Get detections for this species
    detections <- brd_species %>%
      group_by(siteID, year) %>%
      summarize(present = 1, .groups = "drop")
    
    # Build site-year detection matrix
    current_site_by_year <- valid_site_years %>%
      left_join(detections, by = c("siteID", "year")) %>%
      mutate(present = replace_na(present, 0)) %>%
      pivot_wider(
        names_from = year,
        values_from = present
      )
    
    # Create Pao object
    birds_pao <- createPao(
      data = site_by_year[, years],
      unitnames = site_by_year$siteID,
      title = common_name
    )
    
    # Run occupancy model
    model <- occMod(
      data = birds_pao,
      model = list(psi ~ 1, p ~ 1),
      type = "so"
    )
    
    # Extract estimates
    ests <- print_one_site_estimates(mod = model) %>%
      as.data.frame() %>%
      slice(1:2)
    
    rownames(ests) <- NULL
    
    named_est <- list(
      vernacularName = common_name,
      psi_Estimate = ests$est[1],
      psi_SE       = ests$se[1],
      psi_L95      = ests$lower[1],
      psi_U95      = ests$upper[1],
      p_Estimate   = ests$est[2],
      p_SE         = ests$se[2],
      p_L95        = ests$lower[2],
      p_U95        = ests$upper[2]
    )

    detection_histories[[sci_name]] <- site_by_year
    results[[sci_name]] <- named_est
  }
  
  return(list(
    estimates = results,
    detection_histories = detection_histories
  ))
  
}
```

We will now run the function for all species. 

```{r warning=FALSE}
species_input <- brd_joineddata_clean %>%
  distinct(scientificName, vernacularName) %>%
  arrange(scientificName)

results_df <- run_occ_for_species_list(
  species_df = species_input,
  brd_joineddata_clean = brd_joineddata_clean,
  brd_perpoint_clean = brd_perpoint_clean,
  sites = sites
)
```

#### Results
Using the function defined above, we fit single-season occupancy models for all bird species observed in the dataset. For each species, we estimated occupancy probability and detection probability.


Plot psi (occupancy)

```{r}
psi_df <- bind_rows(lapply(names(results_df$estimates), function(name) {
  row <- results_df$estimates[[name]]
  tibble(
    scientificName = name,
    vernacularName = row$vernacularName,
    psi_Estimate = row$psi_Estimate,
    psi_SE = row$psi_SE,
    psi_L95 = row$psi_L95,
    psi_U95 = row$psi_U95
  )
})) %>%
  arrange(psi_Estimate)

psi_df <- psi_df %>%
  mutate(label = paste0(scientificName))
  #mutate(label = paste0(scientificName, "\n", vernacularName))

ggplot(psi_df, aes(x = reorder(label, psi_Estimate), y = psi_Estimate)) +
  geom_col(fill = "grey") +
  geom_errorbar(aes(ymin = psi_L95, ymax = psi_U95), width = 0.2) +
  labs(
    title = "Species Occupancy (ψ) Estimates",
    x = "Species",
    y = "ψ Estimate"
  ) +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 45, hjust = 1))
```


Plot p (detection)

```{r}
p_df <- bind_rows(lapply(names(results_df$estimates), function(name) {
  row <- results_df$estimates[[name]]
  tibble(
    scientificName = name,
    vernacularName = row$vernacularName,
    p_Estimate = row$p_Estimate,
    p_SE = row$p_SE,
    p_L95 = row$p_L95,
    p_U95 = row$p_U95
  )
})) %>%
  arrange(p_Estimate)

p_df <- p_df %>%
  mutate(label = paste0(scientificName))
  #mutate(label = paste0(scientificName, "\n", vernacularName))

ggplot(p_df, aes(x = reorder(label, p_Estimate), y = p_Estimate)) +
  geom_col(fill = "grey") +
  geom_errorbar(aes(ymin = p_L95, ymax = p_U95), width = 0.2) +
  labs(
    title = "Species Detection Probability (p) Estimates",
    x = "Species",
    y = "p Estimate"
  ) +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 45, hjust = 1))
```

Species with a 1 for occupancy and a 1 for detection are often less informative. These boundary estimates often occur when a species is detected in every survey where it occurs, providing little information to estimate imperfect detection. 

```{r eval=FALSE, include=FALSE}
#species with highest psi
psi_df %>%
  arrange(desc(psi_Estimate)) %>%
  head(10)

#species with lowest psi
psi_df %>%
  arrange(psi_Estimate) %>%
  head(10)

#species with highest p
p_df %>%
  arrange(desc(p_Estimate)) %>%
  head(10)

#species with lowest p
p_df %>%
  arrange(p_Estimate) %>%
  head(10)

#look at the presence/absence data
View(results_df$detection_histories$`Sialia currucoides`)

#look at the raw data
View(brd_joineddata_clean %>%
  filter(scientificName == "Melanerpes carolinus"))

#look at the model results
View(results_df$estimates$`Falco peregrinus`)
```

To explore how detection probability varies among species with similar occupancy, we subset species within a narrow range of ψ values and compare their detection estimates.

```{r}
estimates_df <- bind_rows(lapply(names(results_df$estimates), function(name) {
  row <- results_df$estimates[[name]]
  tibble(
    scientificName = name,
    vernacularName = row$vernacularName,
    psi_Estimate = row$psi_Estimate,
    psi_L95 = row$psi_L95,
    psi_U95 = row$psi_U95,
    p_Estimate = row$p_Estimate,
    p_L95 = row$p_L95,
    p_U95 = row$p_U95
  )
}))

psi_range_species <- estimates_df %>%
  filter(psi_Estimate >= 0.5, psi_Estimate <= 0.6) %>%
  select(scientificName, vernacularName, psi_Estimate, p_Estimate, p_L95, p_U95) %>%
  arrange(desc(p_Estimate))

psi_range_species
```
In this example, Blue Jays and Great Horned Owls have similar occupancy probabilities (.51 and .52), yet their detection probabilities differ dramatically (.91 and .23). Blue Jays are highly detectable during point-count surveys, whereas Great Horned Owls are much more difficult to detect under the same protocol.

### Adding Covariates

Detectability and occupancy of a species can be influenced by many different random effects, such as:

Survey characteristics:

* The observer: some observers may be better at spotting individuals of a species that are particularly camouflaged to their environments

* The weather: adverse weather conditions such as rain or snow can impact visibility during a study, and therefore impact detection probability

Site characteristics: sites with heavy cover or dense forests may decrease detection probability and make it harder for observers to identify the species

* Example: Sitka black-tailed deer that live in the boreal forests in southeast Alaska may be harder to spot than mule deer living in more open ecosystems in Nevada

We can include data about these characteristics in our model to either a) describe previously known variation and thereby improve the model fit or b) test to see whether occupancy/detection of a site is a function of a covariate.

#### Occupancy Covariates
These are covariates that influence occupancy of a species. Occupancy probability can only be influenced by site characteristics.

For example, shorebird occupancy would benefit from data on the extent of tidal flats, seabirds distributions are often influenced by ocean depth, and in many regions elevation plays a critical role in determining site occupancy.

Melanerpes carolinus (Red-bellied Woodpecker) across all sites

##### Covariants
We use the same occupancy table as above, but we need to create a table with the site covariates (aka nlcdClass).

```{r}
#categorical
#site_cov <- brd_perpoint_clean %>%
#  select(siteID, nlcdClass) %>%
#  distinct(siteID, .keep_all = TRUE) %>%
#  mutate(nlcdClass = as.factor(nlcdClass)) %>%
#  tibble::column_to_rownames("siteID")

#non-categorical
site_cov <- brd_perpoint_clean %>%
  select(siteID, elevation) %>%
  distinct(siteID, .keep_all = TRUE) %>%
  tibble::column_to_rownames("siteID")
```

#### Create the Pao presence-absence object (Pao)
```{r}
birds_pao_model2 <- createPao(
  data = site_by_year[, c("2018", "2019", "2020", "2021", "2022", "2023")],
  unitnames = site_by_year$siteID,
  unitcov = site_cov,
  title = "Red-bellied Woodpecker"
)
```

#### Run the actual model
```{r}
birds_occupancy_model2 <- occMod(
  data = birds_pao_model2,           
  model = list(psi ~ elevation,  p ~ 1),
  type = 'so'
  )
```

#### Model Results

```{r}
mod.list <-  list(
    birds_occupancy_model1, 
    birds_occupancy_model2
)
aictable <- createAicTable(mod.list = mod.list)
aictable$table
```
Looking at the two models, we can briefly look at the AIC values. The AIC for the model with elevation is lower (better), so the principle of parsimony suggests this is the better model: it is the more parsimonous model when considering both fit and number of parameters.

We see that compared to the original model that did not account for elevation there are 3 parameters vs 2. We can calculate a p value to quantify how much better of a fit this model is.

```{r}
#get the difference in the neg2loglike between the two models
diff <- abs(birds_occupancy_model1$neg2loglike - birds_occupancy_model2$neg2loglike)

#look up our observed difference on a chi-square distribution with 1 degree of freedom to get p value
pchisq(diff, df = 1, lower.tail = FALSE)

```

A p value of 2.356024e-05 is low so we can confidently reject the null hypothesis.

```{r}
coef(birds_occupancy_model2, param = 'psi')

data <- cbind(site_cov, birds_occupancy_model2$real$psi) %>% 
  distinct(.keep_all = TRUE) %>%
  arrange(elevation)

ggplot(data, aes(x = elevation, y = est)) +
  geom_point() + 
  labs(x = "Elevation",
       y = "Predicted Occupancy") +
  lims(y = c(0, 1))
```

#### Detection Covariates
Detection probability can vary not only due to observer skill but also due to environmental conditions that affect animal behavior or survey conditions. For vocal birds, wind speed, temperature, and humidity can strongly influence calling behavior and sound transmission.

It is important to recognize that detection probability can be influenced by either survey characteristics or site characteristics. We are going to see whether temperature of the survey affects the detection of calling Red-bellied Woodpeckers.

#### Data Munging

##### Occupancy Table
We will once more construct an occupancy table, but instead of rows representing sites, we will use plots. This is because a single survey only covers a plot, not an entire site.

```{r}
# Filter table by species
bird_species <- "Setophaga virens"

#unique(brd_joineddata_clean$detectionMethod)

brd_joineddata_model3 <- brd_joineddata_clean %>%
  filter(siteID %in% large_sites) %>%
  filter(scientificName == bird_species) %>%
  filter(detectionMethod %in% c("singing", "calling", "other aural (e.g. wing beats)", "drumming", "calling and singing", "other aural and singing"))

# Get all valid surveys years across plots (so we can fill in NAs)
valid_plot_years <- brd_perpoint_clean %>%
  filter(siteID %in% large_sites) %>%
  distinct(plotID, year)
  
# Get detections — only species *actually observed at a plot* (so we can fill in 0s)
detections <- brd_joineddata_model3 %>%
  filter(siteID %in% large_sites) %>%
  group_by(plotID, year) %>%
  summarize(present = 1, .groups = "drop")
  
# Join and fill
plot_by_year <- valid_plot_years %>%
  left_join(detections, by = c("plotID","year")) %>%
  mutate(present = replace_na(present, 0)) %>%
  pivot_wider(
    names_from = year,
    values_from = present
  ) %>%
  select(1, sort(names(.)[-1])) %>%
  arrange(plotID)

head(plot_by_year, n=10)

```

##### Covariants
NEON bird surveys record environmental conditions at the start and end of each point-count survey. Because multiple point counts occur within a plot and year, we summarize these variables by taking the mean value across all point-count surveys conducted within each plot–year combination.

Below, we construct several candidate detection covariates commonly hypothesized to influence detectability of landbirds:
* Observed air temperature
* Wind speed
* Cloud cover
* Relative humidity

Each covariate is organized as a matrix with rows corresponding to plots and columns corresponding to survey years, matching the structure required by RPresence

Observed air temperature (°C)
```{r}
observedAirTemp_surveys <- brd_joineddata_clean %>% #this needs to be from the whole dataset, since environmental variables are not dependent on bird detection
  filter(siteID %in% large_sites) %>%
  group_by(plotID, year) %>%
  summarize(
    observedAirTemp = na_if(mean(observedAirTemp, na.rm = TRUE), NaN),
    .groups = "drop"
  ) %>%
  pivot_wider(
    names_from = year,
    values_from = observedAirTemp
  ) %>%
  tibble::column_to_rownames('plotID') %>%
  select(sort(names(.)))

```

Wind speed (km/hour)
```{r}
kmPerHourObservedWindSpeed_surveys <- brd_joineddata_clean %>% #this needs to be from the whole dataset, since environmental variables are not dependent on bird detection
  filter(siteID %in% large_sites) %>%
  group_by(plotID, year) %>%
  summarize(
    kmPerHourObservedWindSpeed = na_if(mean(kmPerHourObservedWindSpeed, na.rm = TRUE), NaN),
    .groups = "drop"
  ) %>%
  pivot_wider(
    names_from = year,
    values_from = kmPerHourObservedWindSpeed
  ) %>%
  tibble::column_to_rownames('plotID') %>%
  select(sort(names(.)))

```

Cloud cover percentage
```{r}
cloudCover_surveys <- brd_perpoint_clean %>% #this needs to be from the whole dataset, since environmental variables are not dependent on bird detection
  filter(siteID %in% large_sites) %>%
  group_by(plotID, year) %>%
  summarize(
    cloudCover = na_if(mean((startCloudCoverPercentage + endCloudCoverPercentage) / 2, na.rm = TRUE), NaN),
    .groups = "drop"
  ) %>%
  pivot_wider(
    names_from  = year,
    values_from = cloudCover
  ) %>%
  tibble::column_to_rownames('plotID') %>%
  select(sort(names(.)))
```

Relative humidity (%RH)
```{r}
relativeHumidity_surveys <- brd_perpoint_clean %>% #this needs to be from the whole dataset, since environmental variables are not dependent on bird detection
  filter(siteID %in% large_sites) %>%
  group_by(plotID, year) %>%
  summarize(
    relativeHumidity = na_if(mean((startRH + endRH) / 2, na.rm = TRUE), NaN),
    .groups = "drop"
  ) %>%
  pivot_wider(
    names_from  = year,
    values_from = relativeHumidity
  ) %>%
  tibble::column_to_rownames('plotID') %>%
  select(sort(names(.)))

```

We combine all candidate detection covariates into a single survey-level covariate table. Individual models then specify which covariates are used to explain detection probability, allowing straightforward comparison among alternative detection hypotheses.

```{r}
# create the surveycov dataframe
surveycov <-  data.frame(
  observedAirTemp = unlist(observedAirTemp_surveys),
  kmPerHourObservedWindSpeed = unlist(kmPerHourObservedWindSpeed_surveys),
  cloudCover = unlist(cloudCover_surveys),
  relativeHumidity = unlist(relativeHumidity_surveys)
  )

# remove the rownames
row.names(surveycov) <- NULL

head(surveycov)

```

#### Create the Pao presence-absence object (Pao)
```{r}
birds_pao_model3 <- createPao(
  data = plot_by_year[, c("2018", "2019", "2020", "2021", "2022", "2023")],
  unitnames = plot_by_year$plotID,
  survcov = surveycov,
  title = "Red-Bellied Woodpecker"
)
```

#### Run the actual model
There will be a warning since we are missing some env variable values where we have detection data (i guess for some reason they didn't record it sometimes)
```{r}
birds_occupancy_model3 <- occMod(
  data = birds_pao_model3,           
  model = list(psi ~ 1,  p ~ kmPerHourObservedWindSpeed),
  type = 'so'
  )

summary(birds_occupancy_model3)
```

#### Model Results

```{r}
coef(birds_occupancy_model3, 'p')
```
Here, we can see that the beta estimate for kmPerHourObservedWindSpeed is slightly negative (i.e., as windspeed increases, detection for calling birds decreases) and 0 is not included in the confidence interval, so there is a statistically significant effect that windspeed affects detection

Remember, these coefficients are on the (unbounded) logit scale. The standard error is provided for each estimate, as are the 95% confidence intervals. The confidence intervals can be computed by hand as the estimate +/- 1.96 times the standard error. If the confidence interval encompasses 0, traditionally we say the estimate is “not statistically significant”. If the beta could reasonably be 0, it means the variable has no effect (or at least we don’t have evidence of its effect in the dataset).

Let's plot the effect of wind speed on detection:
```{r}
newdata <- data.frame(
  kmPerHourObservedWindSpeed = seq(from = min(unlist(kmPerHourObservedWindSpeed_surveys), na.rm = TRUE),
             to = max(unlist(kmPerHourObservedWindSpeed_surveys), na.rm = TRUE),
             by = 1)
  )
predictions <- predict(birds_occupancy_model3, newdata, 'p')
predictions$kmPerHourObservedWindSpeed <- newdata$kmPerHourObservedWindSpeed
  
# plot the predictions with ggplot2
ggplot(data = predictions, aes(x = kmPerHourObservedWindSpeed, y = est)) +
 geom_line() +
 geom_line(aes(x = kmPerHourObservedWindSpeed, y = lower_0.95), linetype = "dashed") +
 geom_line(aes(x = kmPerHourObservedWindSpeed, y = upper_0.95), linetype = "dashed") +
 labs(x = "kmPerHourObservedWindSpeed", 
      y = "Predicted detection") +
 lims(y = c(0, 1))
```

###  Multi-season Occupancy Model

While the single-season occupancy model assumes that the sites are closed to changes in occupancy state over the study, we may want to know how occupancy rates are changing over time. For this we use the multi-season occupancy model. Sampling is divided into primary and secondary periods, between which previously occupied sites can go locally extinct, and previously unoccupied sites can be colonized. 

Sampling is divided into:
* Primary periods (e.g., years), between which occupancy status may change
* Secondary periods (e.g., repeated surveys within a year), during which occupancy is assumed to be constant

This structure allows us to estimate not only occupancy and detection, but also colonization and local extinction probabilities. The dynamic occupancy model provides estimates for four key parameters: initial occupancy (ψ), colonization (γ), local extinction (ε), and detection probability (p).

#### Single Species

We will now examine Melanerpes carolinus (Red-bellied Woodpecker) across all sites, now using a multi-season model.

#### Data Munging

##### Occupancy Table
For the multi-season model, each year is treated as a primary season, and the two survey bouts within each year serve as secondary surveys. Detection histories are therefore organized as site × (year × bout) matrices.

```{r}
# Filter table by species
bird_species <- "Melanerpes carolinus"
brd_joineddata_model4 <- brd_joineddata_clean %>%
  filter(siteID %in% small_sites) %>%
  filter(scientificName == bird_species)

brd_joineddata_model4$year_bout <- paste(brd_joineddata_model4$year, brd_joineddata_model4$boutNumber, sep = "_")

head(brd_joineddata_model4)

# Get all valid surveys years across sites (so we can fill in NAs)
valid_site_years <- brd_perpoint_clean %>%
  distinct(siteID, year, boutNumber)

# Get detections — only species *actually observed at a site* (so we can fill in 0s)
detections <- brd_joineddata_model4 %>%
  group_by(siteID, year_bout) %>%
  summarize(present = 1, .groups = "drop")


# Get all valid surveys years across sites (so we can fill in NAs)
valid_site_years <- brd_perpoint_clean %>%
  filter(siteID %in% small_sites) %>%
  distinct(siteID, year, boutNumber)

valid_site_years$year_bout <- paste(valid_site_years$year, valid_site_years$boutNumber, sep = "_")
valid_site_years_bout <- subset(valid_site_years, select = -c(year, boutNumber))


# Get detections — only species *actually observed at a site* (so we can fill in 0s)
detections <- brd_joineddata_model4 %>%
  group_by(siteID, year_bout) %>%
  summarize(present = 1, .groups = "drop")

# Join and fill
site_by_year <- valid_site_years_bout %>%
  left_join(detections, by = c("siteID", "year_bout")) %>%
  mutate(present = replace_na(present, 0)) %>%
  
  pivot_wider(
    names_from = year_bout,
    values_from = present
  )


head(site_by_year, n=10)
```

#### Create the Pao presence-absence object (Pao)
When creating the PAO object, we specify the number of secondary surveys per primary season using the nsurveyseason argument. In this case, each year contains two surveys.

```{r}
birds_pao_model4 <- createPao(
  data = site_by_year[, c("2018_1", "2018_2","2019_1","2019_2", "2020_1","2020_2", "2021_1","2021_2", "2022_1", "2022_2", "2023_1", "2023_2")],
  nsurveyseason = c(2,2,2,2,2,2),
  unitnames = site_by_year$siteID,
  title = "Red-bellied Woodpecker"
)
```

#### Run the actual model
We fit a dynamic occupancy model in which all parameters are assumed to be constant across sites and years:

```{r}
birds_occupancy_model4 <- occMod(
  data = birds_pao_model4,           
  model = list(
    psi ~ 1,  
    epsilon ~ 1,
    gamma ~ 1,
    p ~ 1),
  type = 'do.1'
)

summary(birds_occupancy_model4)
```
This model provides a baseline description of occupancy dynamics, against which more complex models could be compared.

#### Model Results
initial occupancy probability (ψ) 47% (i.e., if you go to any of these sites, there is a 47% chance of this bird occupying the site), a colonization probability (γ): 55% (i.e. previously unoccupied sites had a 55% chance of being colonized the next year), a local extinction (ε) probability of 53% (e.i. occupied sites had a 53% chance of going extinct by the next year), and a detection probability (p) of 47% (i.e., if you visit a site and the bird occupies it, there is a 47% chance you will detect it)

```{r}
ests <- as.data.frame(print_one_site_estimates(mod = birds_occupancy_model4))

ests <- ests[1:4,] %>% 
  mutate(parm = c("psi", "gamma", "epsilon", "p")) %>% 
  select(parm, est, se, lower, upper) %>% 
  rename(., 
    c(
      Parameter = parm,
      Estimate = est,
      SE = se,
      L95 = lower,
      U95 = upper
    )
  ) %>% 
  `rownames<-`(seq_len(nrow(ests[1:4,])))

coef(birds_occupancy_model4, param = 'psi')
```

```{r}
ggplot(ests, aes(x = Parameter, y = Estimate)) +
  labs(x = "Parameter", y = "Estimate") +
  geom_bar(stat = 'identity') +
  geom_errorbar(aes(ymin = L95, ymax = U95), width = 0.2) +
  theme_bw()
```
